articles.title: IRGC Navy intercepts two vessels in southern waters of Hormuz
articles.summary:
IRGC Navy intercepts two vessels in southern waters of Hormuz

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Friday that it halted two tankers in the southern waters of the Strait of Hormuz after they attempted to pass through an unauthorised route.

In a statement, the IRGC Navy said the vessels, one in the eastern and the other in the western part of the strait, had switched off their navigation and positioning systems and ignored several radio warnings.

It accused the US military of supporting the attempted passage and blamed what it called hostile US actions, along with the vessels’ disregard for Iranian regulations, for the incidents and fires aboard the ships.  

The IRGC Navy also said another vessel that caught fire in the southern waters of the strait on Thursday night had sunk.

articles.title: Israeli election bribery probe ‘limited’ and won't affect results, Shin Bet sources say
articles.summary:
Israeli election bribery probe ‘limited’ and won't affect results, Shin Bet sources say

Submitted by MEE staff on Fri, 10/30/2026 - 09:56
Security officials play down allegations of foreign interference as Netanyahu’s Likud party claims Palestinian citizens helped ‘steal’ the election
Head of the Shin Bet domestic security service David Zini participates in a state memorial ceremony for the fallen soldiers at the Mount Herzl military cemetery in Jerusalem on 16 October 2025 (Olivier fitoussi/AFP)
Off

The investigation into suspected Israeli election fraud is limited in scope and unlikely to affect the results, security sources and a senior election official said on Thursday.

Israel’s domestic intelligence agency, Shin Bet, said in an official statement that the investigation was “targeted and limited”.

Channel 12 quoted agency sources as saying the matter under investigation could not affect the election results.

Separately, Dean Livne, acting director general of the Central Elections Committee, said there was “no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity”.

The statements came after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party claimed the election had been “stolen” by Palestinian citizens of Israel following their record turnout and electoral gains.

Likud warned of an attempted “Islamisation of Israel” after reports emerged that Shin Bet was investigating suspected foreign interference in the vote.

The investigation centres on alleged funding efforts to increase turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Israeli politicians and media outlets aligned with the government accused Qatar of providing the funding. Doha rejected the allegations, calling them “ridiculous and dangerous”.

Palestinian-led parties also denied any involvement. They accused Netanyahu of running an incitement campaign against them.

The parties, which contested the election on two separate slates, Ra'am and the Joint List, won 19 seats, potentially giving them a decisive role in coalition negotiations.

Limited probe

Shin Bet said its findings would be presented to the Central Elections Committee once the investigation was complete.

It stressed that the inquiry focused on individuals rather than an entire section of society.

“It should be emphasised that this type of investigation is also targeted and limited, and it should not be used to cast suspicion or accuse an entire segment of the population that voted democratically and legally,” the agency said.

“Only those who acted in violation of the law will be addressed.” 

The agency added that Netanyahu and opposition leaders Gadi Eisenkot and Yair Lapid had been personally briefed on the main allegations under investigation.

Following the briefing, Lapid said the allegations were unlikely to affect the election results.

Why Palestinian electoral gains in Israel should be met with caution, not celebration
Read More »

The evidence did not justify challenging the outcome or delaying the swearing-in of the new Knesset, he added. 

“Based on my familiarity with the material and the opinion of authorities dealing with the matter, there is no risk to challenge the election results, and there is no impediment to swearing in the Knesset,” Lapid said on X.

Eisenkot, leader of the main opposition bloc and a candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, accused Likud of running a campaign to undermine the election results.

“It is already clear that Likud and Netanyahu have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election,” he said.

Likud had urged Zionist opposition parties to rule out any agreement with the Palestinian-led electoral slates.

“After it was revealed that foreign entities tried to take over the Knesset, it is clear that no Zionist party should cooperate with Ra'am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker through votes bought for cash, and form a government that is dangerous to Israel,” the party said.

The statement came after Ahmad Tibi, a Joint List member of the Knesset, told Israeli Army Radio that opposition figures had approached him about replacing Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a Likud lawmaker.

Tibi did not identify the party involved but said several potential replacements had been discussed.

“We support replacing the Knesset speaker. That is something an opposition does after an election... I think the right thing to do is to take this step,” he said.

articles.title: More than 100 ports join international dockworkers’ strike against arms shipments
articles.summary:
More than 100 ports join international dockworkers’ strike against arms shipments

Dockworkers across Europe are staging strikes and demonstrations as part of an international campaign against arms shipments and port militarisation.

Unions in France, Italy, Greece, Spain, Turkey and Morocco have called for an end to wars in the Middle East, including Gaza. 

“Ports must not be used for the transport of weapons, ammunition, military equipment and troops,” a joint statement said. “Dockworkers do not work for war!”

In Greece, the Enedep union called a strike at Piraeus, while Italy’s USB announced demonstrations in Genoa, Trieste and Gioia Tauro. 

France’s CGT ports and docks federation called a one-day strike at major ports, including Le Havre, Marseille, Dunkirk and Rouen.

articles.title: Exclusive: Miliband set on sanctions regardless of Israel election outcome as officials try to weaken measures
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Miliband set on sanctions regardless of Israel election outcome as officials try to weaken measures

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Fri, 10/30/2026 - 09:21
The foreign secretary is understood to be determined that sanctions should not be watered down
Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband (AFP)
Off

Britain will press ahead with sanctions on Israeli settlements whatever the outcome of Israel's elections, senior UK government figures have privately insisted.

Even if Benjamin Netanyahu is no longer prime minister, Labour ministers intend to implement comprehensive sanctions, including against companies providing construction and real estate services for settlement expansion.

Implementing the sanctions, however, will not be an easy task and the process could take up to nine months.

Speaking to Middle East Eye, multiple government and Labour sources accused some civil servants of causing “blockages” and attempting to weaken the sanctions.

Within the Foreign Office, MEE understands, some officials have been pushing for the sanctions to target Israeli companies complicit in the illegal settlements but not British companies that are complicit. 

Officials have also argued that companies that operate mostly within Israel itself, as well as in occupied Palestinian territory, should not be impacted by the sanctions. 

This would mean a weakening of the sanctions announced by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in September, restricting their focus to companies that operate mostly in illegal settlements.

Exclusive: London event advertises Israeli agency building illegal settlements
Read More »

Uncertainty lingers over some of the measures that Miliband announced in September. He said the sanctions regime would include “appropriate religious exemptions”, but it has not been publicly made clear what these exemptions are and how extensive they will be. 

In August, the Charity Commission opened an investigation after Labour MP Melanie Ward said at least 32 charities registered in England and Wales had transferred more than £28m to Israeli settlements.

“The Foreign Office is worried that pro-Israel groups could mount legal challenges to try and disrupt the sanctions,” one source said. “This helps explain how cautious some of the civil servants are.”

The British embassy in Tel Aviv is reported to have been opposed to the sanctions in the first place. 

However, Miliband himself is understood to be determined that the sanctions regime should not be watered down.

Could the Israeli elections change the equation?

When Miliband announced the sanctions on 8 September in parliament, he insisted that “I do not want to, in any sense, interfere in that election. The election is for the Israeli people to make their own decisions about their future. 

“I have set out the policy of the British government, and I have made it clear that our quarrel is not with the Israeli people but with the policies of the Netanyahu government.”

Relations between the UK and the Netanyahu government have deteriorated in the past two months, with Israel forcing Britain to downgrade its consulate in occupied East Jerusalem to the status of a mission in retaliation for Labour's sanctions.

This week the British government confirmed it has paused cooperation with Israel under the 2030 roadmap for bilateral relations - a strategic agreement signed in 2023 under the Conservative government, and shortly after a new Israeli government under Netanyahu entered power.

If implemented fully, the new sanctions would require British banks, pension funds and asset managers to divest from companies operating in settlements.

They would also stop financial institutions from providing mortgages, insurance and other services that support settlement activity.

Israeli elections and E1 settlement plan

The Burnham government’s timing in announcing its sanctions was in part motivated by a sense of urgency because of the E1 settlement plan, MEE understands. 

The E1 plan involves building thousands of new housing units between Jerusalem and the existing West Bank settlement of Maale Adumim, 7 km east of the city.

It would effectively cut the West Bank in half, making a Palestinian state unviable.

Critics of the sanctions said they were “performative”, but they appear to have had an immediate effect in Israel itself. 

Another East Jerusalem neighbourhood is demolished as the world fails to act
Read More »

After the sanctions were unveiled, Israel's attorney general ordered that the announcement of the winning bidders for E1 settlement tenders be postponed until after the elections.

The Israeli elections have resulted in a deadlock between Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition.

Palestinian-led parties have offered to support an opposition-led minority government to prevent Netanyahu from returning to power. But key opposition figures have rejected the idea of governing with Arab parties.

Negotiations have now begun to form a “national unity” government through a power-sharing arrangement between Netanyahu and major opposition parties.

Gadi Eisenkot, head of the opposition Yashar party, has vocally opposed E1, but still supports settlements in East Jerusalem and the West Bank - all of which are illegal under international law - in general. 

British ministers are understood to believe that even if the next Israeli government drops the E1 plan this should not affect the sanctions, which are designed to bring Britain into line with international law. 

But what the sanctions will actually look like - and whether they match up to the foreign secretary’s original announcement on 8 September - remains to be seen.

UK Politics
Peter Oborne
